title: Paste a generated repair payload — never re-type it; the hand is the untrusted transport
statement: When a repair payload has been generated from canonical source data, PASTE it into the tool call — never re-type or re-transcribe it. The hand is the untrusted transport: re-typing reintroduces exactly the class of error the generator existed to remove. And end every repair spanning more than one row with an INDEPENDENT re-read that re-derives each expected value from its source, because care does not catch a transcription error — only a verifier does.
context: The tamheed 4.2.0 register repair (PE-336; findings_18 §1). Recovering probability and impact for all 23 risk rows, every payload was correctly BUILT BY SCRIPT from data/*.jsonl rather than from entity_query output — the rule that was already on the books, and it was followed. Transcribing the generator's output into the entity_upsert call, I typed RISK-012's probability as `medium` where the stash said H -> high. The generator was right for all 23 rows; the transport corrupted one. What caught it was NOT care — I was being careful, and care missed it — but a verifier that re-read the JSONL after the write and re-derived every expected value from the stash independently, which named the offending row in one line.
recommendation: 1. Build the payload from the canonical files (`data/*.jsonl`), never from an `entity_query` round-trip — the store holds truncated rows and v4 demands full ones. 2. Move it into the call by PASTE, not by hand. 3. Where a paste is structurally impossible — an MCP tool call whose arguments must be composed rather than pasted — treat the composition as untrusted and make step 4 mandatory rather than optional. 4. End any repair over N>1 rows with an independent verifier that re-reads the canonical file and re-derives each expected value from its own source; ASSERT the comparison, never eyeball it. Save a pre-image before the write so the verifier has something to compare against.
rationale: A generator's correctness does not survive manual re-transcription: generation and transport are two steps and only the first is mechanical. The failure is silent by construction — a plausible value in a plausible field — so nothing downstream refuses it, and re-reading your own transcription recruits the same faculty that produced the error. Only a re-derivation from the source has the property that it cannot repeat the mistake, which is why the verifier and not the vigilance is the control.
impact_if_followed: A multi-row repair's correctness rests on two mechanical things — the generator and the verifier — rather than on the hand between them. Demonstrated on the 4.2.0 re-run: scale mismatches NONE, lost stash NONE, titles byte-identical to v1.Risk, milestones 6/6 with the v1 blob preserved. The cost is one extra script. Demonstrated again on 2026-08-15 closing DEF-056: a 3102-character defect title was re-sent and verified verbatim against a pre-image, and the same discipline surfaced a hand-invented `found_in` value that the store's FK then refused.
impact_if_ignored: A silently corrupted row enters an append-only record wearing a plausible value that no gate can refuse. Every mechanical gate here is ROW-LEVEL, which is exactly how the v2.3 migration passed 7/7 while damaging register data at COLUMN level. RISK-012 would have carried a wrong probability into every later risk review, and `risk-liveness` — whose predicate reads probability and impact — would have evaluated the wrong row without failing, the hollow-pass shape all over again.

title: Ask every time — a previously given answer is evidence about the past, never consent for the present
statement: When a decision belongs to the operator, run the interview EVERY time. Do not bank their earlier answers as a starting position, a default, or a shortcut for a later ceremony. An answer given in one context is evidence of what was true then; it is never authorisation for now. Where a record must carry a past answer, mark it explicitly as history that does NOT relieve the next session of asking.
context: 2026-08-16, the first `skill-promote` ceremony. The ceremony was run correctly — candidates clustered, the pinned-lesson graduation warning given, a straw-man offered, and a hard STOP at the operator's cluster pick — and the operator DECLINED. Alongside the decline they answered two of the interview questions (a name, and a level that went against the recommendation). I recorded those in `PE-368` framed as captured 'so the interview is not re-run from scratch'. The operator rejected that framing outright: 'always you must interview me'. Corrected in `PE-369`. Note that nothing was mis-written and no work was authorised wrongly — the damage was entirely in the RECORD, which would have taught the next session to treat a stale answer as a settled starting point.
recommendation: 1. Treat an operator answer as scoped to the moment it was given — the decision it accompanied, and nothing further. 2. Never carry answers forward as inputs to a future interview, even to be 'efficient'; the efficiency comes out of the operator's authority. 3. When a record must preserve what was said, label it HISTORY and state in the same breath that the next session asks again regardless. 4. Read a ceremony prompt's own stop conditions as binding on the RECORD as well as on the actions: honouring a STOP and then writing a shortcut past it into the journal defeats it one session later. 5. When in doubt about whether something is the operator's to decide, ask — the cost of one question is always lower than the cost of an assumed default.
rationale: Banking an answer silently converts a DECISION into a DEFAULT. The next session reads the captured value, treats it as settled, and the interview the ceremony exists to force degrades into a confirmation of something said once about a different moment — the operator is nominally still consulted while their actual choice has been pre-made. This is the same failure the lesson family itself screens for (persisting an answer as if it remained true), arriving through the journal rather than through a lesson row. It is also why interactive ceremonies place their STOPs where they do: the stop is worthless if the record routes around it.
impact_if_followed: Every operator decision is made in the context it actually applies to, and the record stays a description of what happened rather than a set of pre-loaded answers. Ceremonies keep the property they were designed for — that the operator decides at every step — across session boundaries, which is the only place that property can be lost.
impact_if_ignored: A stale preference quietly becomes policy. The most likely concrete harm here: a later session opens the promotion, reads a captured name and level, and writes a `SKILL.md` at a level the operator would no longer choose — having been 'consulted' only to confirm their own months-old answer. Worse, the failure is invisible, because the record will show an interview that appeared to happen.

title: Open the interview the moment a decision or an action is the operator's — never surface a blocker and then stand still. Do the homework first, ask simply with examples, and show the entity with its id.
statement: When something needs the OPERATOR — a decision that is theirs to make, or an action only they can perform — START THE INTERVIEW IMMEDIATELY. Do not report the blocker and wait to be asked. FOUR RULES GOVERN HOW IT IS DONE. (1) DO THE HOMEWORK FIRST: gather the facts, read the code, take the measurement, resolve everything that is resolvable, so the operator is DECIDING rather than researching. Never ask a question whose answer is already in the repository. (2) ASK CLEARLY AND SIMPLY, WITH EXAMPLES: one decision per question, plain language, and a concrete illustration of what each option means in practice. (3) DISPLAY THE ENTITY WITH ITS ID: quote what the row actually says — its text, severity, status — AND keep the identifier alongside it, so the decision can be made from the message itself while the id remains the handle for looking it up, quoting it back, and tracing it. Neither half alone is enough: an id without content makes the reader fetch the record, and content without an id makes the claim uncheckable. This applies to DEF-, DEC-, ADR-, AC-, RISK- and every other family. (4) ASKING EARLY IS NOT A LICENCE TO REUSE (LL-002): every ceremony still gets its own fresh interview.
context: 2026-08-16, given by the operator during the DEF-078 readiness work. Across that session the agent repeatedly did the right analysis and then STOPPED at the edge of the operator's authority — surfacing the UAT credential rotation (blocked on a stopped instance), the gitleaks allowlist narrowing (blocked on docs triage), and the startup-interlock consequence of DEC-056 d2 — and in each case wrote 'this is your call' and waited instead of putting the question. The operator had to prompt for the interview. Nothing was decided wrongly; the cost was pure latency and an unfinished turn, repeatedly. The same session also showed the presentation failure: blockers were cited as bare identifiers ('DEF-081 is filed high'), which forces the reader to open the register to learn what they are being asked about.
recommendation: 1. The moment a blocker is identified as the operator's, ASK — in the same turn, not the next one. 2. Before asking, exhaust what you can determine yourself: run the command, read the config, take the measurement. An interview that offloads research is worse than none. 3. One decision per question; name the options and show what each looks like in practice. 4. Quote the entity's content inline — severity, status, and the sentence that matters — WITH its id: never the id alone, and never the content alone. 5. Where an option carries a risk the operator has not seen, state it inside the option, not after the answer. 6. If several decisions are pending, batch them into one interview rather than trickling them across turns.
rationale: An agent that identifies an operator decision and then waits has converted a two-minute question into an idle turn, and has quietly made a decision of its own — the decision not to ask yet. The operator experiences this as the work stalling for no stated reason. The homework clause is the load-bearing half: asking early is only valuable if the question is fully prepared, because an interview that hands back unresearched options looks like consultation while transferring the work. And an id-only reference has the same defect at the presentation layer — it appears to inform while requiring the reader to do the retrieval, which in practice means the decision gets made on the agent's summary instead of the record. The id must still travel with the content, though: it is the durable handle that makes the summary checkable against the register and citable afterwards, so quoting content without an id trades one presentation failure for another.
category: operator-interaction; interview; blocking; question-quality; entity-presentation; preparation
impact_if_followed: Operator decisions arrive early, fully prepared, and answerable from the message itself. Blocked work either unblocks in the same turn or is explicitly parked BY THE OPERATOR rather than by the agent's silence. The register is read as content rather than as pointers, so a wrong recommendation is visible at the moment of decision.
impact_if_ignored: Work stalls at exactly the points that matter most — the ones needing authority — and the stall is invisible, because the agent's report reads as complete. The most likely concrete harm: a security item like the outstanding UAT credential rotation sits 'surfaced' across several sessions, each one correctly identifying it and none asking the one question that would close it, while the agent's own status reports show it as known and handled.

title: A package-write commit cannot cite itself - reconcile git against the package by CLASSIFYING the unreferenced commits, never by counting them
statement: When cross-checking git against a Tamheed package, a commit whose entire content IS the package write can never contain a reference to its own sha: the MCP write happens FIRST, and the commit carrying the resulting JSONL is created afterwards, so that sha did not exist when the row was written. The raw 'commits with no recorded binding' set is therefore dominated by commits that are correct by construction. NEVER report that raw set as a finding. Classify every unreferenced commit by the PATHS IT TOUCHES - package-only, memory/docs-only, or production code - and flag ONLY the production-code ones. State the discriminator in the report even when the result is empty, so a clean result is legible as a check that RAN rather than a check that was skipped.
context: 2026-08-17 orientation on the ACMP package (PE-415). The orient-resume instruction asks for 'commits that look like package-relevant work but have no recorded binding'. Substring-matching each of the last 25 shas against data/*.jsonl returned 19 unreferenced - 76% of the window. Reporting that list would have been 18 false alarms, and the prompt's own wording invites the error: a `chore(tamheed)` commit IS package-relevant work under any plain reading. One `git show --name-only` per commit resolved it in a single pass - 18 touched only tamheed-package/**, one touched only a memory file, and the single production-code commit in the window (8eba85a, PR #288) was correctly bound under DW-026. The nearly-made mistake was not a wrong conclusion but a wrong REPORT: handing the operator 19 identifiers to research.
recommendation: 1. Match each commit's short AND full sha against all data/*.jsonl mechanically - never judge from commit messages, which say 'DEF-084' whether or not anything was bound. 2. For every unreferenced commit run `git show --name-only` and bucket by path prefix: tamheed-package/** = self-referentially unbindable, expected clean; memory/docs-only = out of scope; anything under src/ or tests/ = a real candidate. 3. Flag bucket 3 ONLY. 4. Report the discriminator alongside the result - 'none, because every unreferenced commit is a package write, which cannot cite itself' is a check; a bare 'no findings' is indistinguishable from not having looked. 5. Never invent a verdict for a bucket-3 commit: name it and let the operator decide.
rationale: The check's raw output has a systematically high false-positive rate that is a property of the RECORDING PROTOCOL itself, not of the repository's health - package writes are always committed after the fact. An agent that reports the raw set trains the operator to ignore the check. An agent that quietly drops it reports 'no unrecorded work' from a check whose output was never interpreted, which is this project's recorded hollow-pass shape arriving at the reporting layer instead of the test layer. The path-prefix classification is the only step that separates the two, and it costs one `git show` per commit.
impact_if_followed: The git-to-package reconciliation stays a LIVE signal: a genuinely unrecorded code commit is visible against a quiet background instead of buried in a list of expected ones, and an empty result carries its own evidence that the instrument had a subject. Demonstrated on 2026-08-17: 25 commits reduced to exactly one production-code commit, checked, and found already bound.
impact_if_ignored: Two opposite failure modes, both bad. Reported raw, the check cries wolf - 19 of 25 commits flagged here - and the operator learns to skip it, so the one genuinely unbound commit eventually arrives inside a list nobody reads. Suppressed, the report asserts 'no unrecorded work' on the strength of an uninterpreted check; this project already records that a clean scan which cannot prove it had a subject is indistinguishable from a clean codebase (the DEF-039 i18n grep that scanned the renamed token, and DEF-056's two NotContain controls that passed vacuously against a column of nulls).

title: Check the register BEFORE offering the operator an option, not after — 'record it as deliberately unexposed' is a silent retirement when an approved requirement already covers the capability
statement: Before asking the operator to dispose of a capability — wire it, drop it, record it as intentional — search the requirement register for a row that already covers it. An option like 'record as deliberately unexposed' silently PRESUMES the capability is unplanned. If an Approved requirement covers it, choosing that option retires approved, traced work by side effect, and the operator cannot see that unless the check was run first. The register sweep is part of the homework LL-003 rule 1 demands, not a follow-up task: an interview option that has not been checked against the plan is not a prepared question, however well the code was read.
context: 2026-08-17, the DEF-084 interview (PE-418, DEC-057). The code homework was thorough — all eight unreachable methods read in source, every caller grepped, three distinct root causes established — and on that basis the operator was asked whether to wire Topic.Convert and Topic.Reclassify or 'record them as deliberately unexposed'. They chose unexposed. Only afterwards, running the FR-coverage check the advisor prompted for, did FR-030 appear: Approved, priority S, sourced to README section E, already traced WBS-5.7 --implements--> and TEST-018 --tests-->, and covering exactly that conversion capability. Applying the answer as given would have abandoned an approved traced requirement by way of a comment in a test-file allowlist. The answer was NOT applied: the fact was surfaced, the question re-put with FR-030 quoted in full, and the operator chose explicit deferral (DW-030). Nothing was mis-written — the cost was one wasted decision and an interview the operator had to make twice.
recommendation: 1. For every capability an interview will ask about, sweep the requirement register (title + statement + rationale) for it BEFORE composing the question — a regex over the canonical requirements.jsonl takes seconds and reads all rows, not the ones you remember. 2. Also check its trace edges: a requirement with implements/tests edges is PLANNED work with a work item and a test row behind it, which is a much stronger claim on the operator's attention than a bare Approved row. 3. Where a requirement exists, the honest options are build / defer with a trigger / retire via scope-change — 'record as unexposed' is not among them, because it changes the plan without a scope-change row. 4. Where no requirement exists, say so explicitly in the option, because that is itself the decision-relevant fact. 5. If the check is run late and contradicts an answer already given, SURFACE IT AND RE-ASK — never apply the answer and note the discrepancy afterwards.
rationale: An interview transfers a decision to the operator, and it can only do that honestly if the options are true. 'Record it as deliberately unexposed' sounds like a no-op — nothing is built, nothing is deleted — which is exactly why it is dangerous: its real effect, when a requirement exists, is to retire that requirement without a scope-change row, without a decision_ref, and without the delta edges the protocol requires. The operator would be agreeing to something the option did not name. This is the same failure shape the project already records at the measurement layer (a control that cannot see its subject) arriving at the INTERVIEW layer: a question that has not been checked against the register is an instrument that cannot detect the case it most needs to catch.
category: operator-interaction; interview; homework; requirement-coverage; scope-change; silent-drift
impact_if_followed: The operator decides on options that are all actually available, and a capability that already has an approved requirement behind it is never disposed of by an allowlist comment. Demonstrated the same day: once FR-030 was quoted in full with its traces, the operator picked a fourth option — explicit deferral with an activation trigger — that the original question had not even offered.
impact_if_ignored: Approved, traced requirements get abandoned invisibly, one interview at a time. The damage is in the RECORD rather than the build, which is what makes it hard to find later: FR-030 would have stayed Approved and traced to WBS-5.7 forever, reading to every future session as planned work, while the only evidence of the decision to drop it sat in a comment inside a test file. That is precisely the drift the standing rule forbids — code and package disagree and neither is fixed nor recorded.

title: A proxy is not the artifact: a register attribute, a register row, and a filename each said BUILT about code that was not
statement: Before classifying something as built, read the thing itself. Every proxy failed in one session, each time while I was correcting the previous proxy's failure: (1) the requirement register's mvp/Phase attributes said 53 requirements were 'deliberately not built' - about 30 were built and shipped, because the attributes record the ORIGINAL scoping and the P1-P19 ladder outgrew them; (2) correcting that, I trusted a DIFFERENT register row (DW-001) and a FILENAME, and reported FR-036 as built because Timeline.tsx exists; (3) reading Timeline.tsx showed a deliberate honest SHELL whose own header says 'no bars are drawn', and the same read caught Calendar.tsx as a second shell. The shells are the sharpest form of this: present, deliberate, well-commented, routed, and empty - every proxy says built, and only the file says otherwise.
context: The DW-029 classification sweep, 2026-08-18, over the 161 requirements with no acceptance criterion. The stakes were real: SC-020 would have stamped live, shipped features 'Deferred', falsifying the register in the opposite direction from the manufactured-status failure DEF-010 records - and the operator approved the reclassification twice against my counts before the shells were found.
recommendation: Classify from source, never from an attribute, a register row, or a path. Check BOTH directions - the sweep found FR-032 unbuilt inside the 'presumed built' group as well as ~30 built inside the 'presumed unbuilt' one. When a proxy is unavoidable, prefer one that is high-precision in a stated direction and say which: requirement ids cited in source comments proved strong evidence of being BUILT, but the instrument is POSITIVE-ONLY (Kanban.tsx plainly exists and is never cited) and one citation turned out to be a DEFERRAL note (InvariantStatus.cs:7). And check that the instrument can discriminate at all: slice status could not classify the 53, because all of them have slice_id NULL and the check returns one bucket whatever the truth is.
impact_if_followed: Classification reflects what exists. The sweep, done properly, also surfaced four requirements unbuilt with NO record anywhere (FR-032, FR-134, FR-154, FR-155), a decision recorded only in a code comment (FR-108/109, now DEC-062), and a deferral whose blocker had silently cleared (FR-035, now DW-037) - none of which any gate could have found.
impact_if_ignored: The register acquires false statuses that no gate can detect, in whichever direction the proxy happens to be wrong. A Deferred label on shipped work is exactly as dishonest as an Implemented label on unbuilt work, and it is harder to notice because it looks conservative.

title: A checker that reports success may have had nothing to check: prove the instrument has a subject before believing its green
statement: Before trusting a clean scan, prove the scanner actually looked at something. Inject a deliberate fault and watch the count move. A tool that exits 0 over an empty file set is indistinguishable, at the exit code, from a tool that exits 0 over a clean one - and the empty case is silent by construction, so nothing will ever tell you.
context: SL-030, 2026-08-19. `npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json` in src/Acmp.Web exited 0 and I recorded the SPA as typechecking. It checks NOTHING: that file is solution-style - "files": [] plus three project references - so tsc resolves zero inputs and succeeds. The tree it blessed had THIRTEEN type errors and had been failing `npm run build` for ten commits (DEF-091). I only caught it because vitest failed seconds later on a change tsc had just approved; had the two agreed, I would have opened a PR asserting a typecheck that never ran. The same session had already been bitten by a sibling of this: `grep -c $'\r'` reported CRs on a pure-LF file, and a control file with one CR line reported two.
recommendation: For any gate you are about to cite as evidence - typecheck, lint, formatter, security scan, coverage - run it once with a deliberate fault present and confirm it FAILS, then remove the fault. Prefer the command CI runs (here `npm run build`) over a hand-rolled invocation, because CI's command is the one whose subject is known-good. Where a config file can be empty-by-design (solution-style tsconfig, an unmatched glob, a filter that selects nothing), treat a pass as unproven until the subject count is visible.
impact_if_followed: A cited gate means what it says. The deliberate-fault check cost about thirty seconds here and converted a false green into DEF-091, which turned out to be a HIGH-severity finding blocking the PR - ten commits of red that four sessions of green vitest runs had hidden.
impact_if_ignored: Evidence that is literally empty gets recorded as verification, in audit rows and PR bodies that later sessions read as settled. It is strictly worse than no check: an absent check invites suspicion, while a passing one closes the question.

title: Sweep the registers by KEYWORD as well as by identifier - an id-only sweep is a scan with no subject when the two rows never name each other
statement: LL-005 and its trap tell you to sweep the adr, decision and open-question registers before disposing of a capability or putting an option in front of the operator. Batch 14 did exactly that for seven candidate requirements, BY IDENTIFIER, and got ZERO hits for six of the seven. That result reads as 'the registers are silent about these' and it is wrong. The keyword sweep run immediately afterwards found decisive governing rows for THREE of them - and one of those, ADR-0035, is Approved and ratified and replaces the storage technology that NFR-027 still mandated by name. NFR-027 says MinIO. ADR-0035 says MinIO. NEITHER ROW CONTAINS THE OTHER'S IDENTIFIER ANYWHERE, so no identifier sweep could ever have connected them, however carefully it was run. THE GENERAL SHAPE: a requirement and the decision that superseded it are usually written years apart by different hands, and cross-references are added only when someone happens to notice the link - which is precisely the noticing this sweep exists to do. Identifiers are how the register refers to itself AFTER the connection is known; the SUBJECT MATTER is what they share BEFORE it is. So sweep on the nouns: the technology, the vendor, the mechanism, the surface. HOW TO APPLY: for each candidate, extract three to six subject keywords from its own statement and grep the adr, decision, open-question, constraint and invariant registers for those as well as for the id. Run BOTH - the id sweep still finds the deliberate cross-references, and it is cheap. And when the id sweep comes back empty for most of a batch, treat that emptiness as a signal the instrument is too narrow rather than as a finding about the registers.

LL-005 says WHICH registers to sweep and was already pinned; batch 13's near-miss extended that from requirements to adrs, decisions and open_questions. This adds HOW to sweep them, which is the half that was still unstated - and batch 14 shows the how can silently defeat the which.", "cost_if_ignored": "Batch 14 would have written an acceptance criterion naming self-hosted MinIO, contradicting a ratified ADR, and recorded it as Met with real-looking evidence for the other three clauses. That is worse than leaving the requirement unverified, because a Met verdict stops anyone looking again."}

title: Two instruments agreeing is ONE instrument when they share a mechanism - corroboration requires independence, not repetition
statement: Verifying that no pre-signed URL can reach a notification, batch 14 wrote a line-based grep for the record's constructor and got 13 construction sites across 7 files. Suspecting the line-based approach, it then wrote a genuinely different instrument - a multi-line-aware argument parser that tracks brackets and string literals - and got THE SAME 13 SITES ACROSS THE SAME 7 FILES. Two independently written scanners, identical answer. That is what corroboration looks like, and it was false: both were blind to the same two builder files, because those use C# target-typed 'new(' where the type is inferred from the return type, so the string the pattern keys on never appears at the construction site at all. TWENTY PERCENT OF THE SURFACE WAS INVISIBLE TO BOTH, and their agreement made that invisibility feel confirmed. THE TEST THAT MATTERS is not 'did I check it twice' but 'do my two checks share a MECHANISM'. Both of these keyed on the same token in the same position; varying the parsing sophistication varied nothing that mattered. THE FIX WAS TO CHANGE THE SUBJECT, not the sophistication: scan every builder FILE for what must not be there - an absolute URL, a storage reference, a non-relative link helper - rather than scanning for a syntactic pattern and enumerating what it finds. A file set is countable and assertable; you can state that there are ten of them and fail if there are fewer. A syntactic pattern silently narrows and its denominator is whatever it happened to match. HOW TO APPLY: prefer an instrument whose subject is an enumerable population over one whose subject is a pattern; assert the population size before believing any result over it; and when a second instrument agrees with the first, ask what they have in common before counting it as evidence.

title: When a requirement says X shall be the single source for Y, check that X EXISTS before measuring anything about Y - a missing ruler makes the measurable half undecidable, not merely unverified
statement: NFR-039 has two clauses: the EN-AR terminology glossary shall be the SINGLE SOURCE of canonical bilingual terms, and no term shall have more than one AR translation in the application. Batch 15 was queued to verify it and the obvious move was to go straight at the second clause, because it is the mechanical one - pair the i18n resource files, group by English label, count distinct Arabic renderings. That measurement runs fine and produces a number. THE NUMBER MEANS NOTHING WITHOUT THE FIRST CLAUSE, and the first clause turned out to be false: README section G lists 22 English terms and says the Arabic pairing is finalized in the design handoff; the design handoff says the shared glossary is README section G; the archived governance glossary says the pairing lives in the design and i18n resources. THREE DOCUMENTS, ZERO ARABIC CHARACTERS BETWEEN THEM, each pointing at another. The glossary does not exist. THE CONSEQUENCE IS SHARPER THAN 'ONE CLAUSE FAILED'. Where two Arabic renderings of one English label genuinely differ, deciding which is canonical requires a canon - and there is none. So the second clause is not unverified, it is UNDECIDABLE, and a verdict citing the measurement would have looked thoroughly evidenced while resting on nothing. THE GENERAL FORM: a requirement of the shape 'X shall be the single source of truth for Y' has a DEPENDENCY ORDER, not two independent clauses. Y is only measurable relative to X. The same shape appears wherever a requirement names a policy, a standard, a glossary, a reference implementation or a baseline as the thing conformance is measured against. HOW TO APPLY: when a requirement names an authority, OPEN THE AUTHORITY FIRST - before writing any instrument for the conformance half. Confirm it exists, that it is not a pointer to something else, and that it actually contains the kind of content the requirement says it holds. If it does not, stop: the conformance half cannot be verified, no acceptance criterion can be written, and the honest instrument is a deferred-work row saying the ruler is missing. A missing authority is a DIFFERENT finding from a half-built feature and should not be filed as one.

title: An identifier is a POINTER, not a reference - any artifact put in front of the operator must carry the full text of every entity it cites, at the point it cites it
statement: THE INSTANCE. Asked to disposition 53 open deferred-work rows, I built a slate that named roughly forty package entities by identifier alone - every DW row by number, plus DEC-064, SC-020, ADR-0022, DEC-020, ADR-0003, OQ-040, AC-049, AC-105, NFR-011, NFR-013, FR-035 and more - and then asked the operator to rule on them. The operator refused the interview and said so plainly: do not just mention an id and expect me to go and check it myself. THE FAILURE IS NOT COSMETIC AND IT IS NOT ABOUT FORMATTING. An identifier is an index into a store the reader may not have open. Citing one transfers the retrieval work to the person the artifact exists to serve, and it does it at the exact moment they are being asked to decide - so the practical effect is either a decision made on my summary of the row rather than the row, or no decision at all. Both are worse than a longer document. WHY IT IS EASY TO GET WRONG. Identifiers read as precision. A slate dense with DEC-064 and ADR-0022 looks rigorous and traceable, and it IS traceable - for the agent, which has the store open and can resolve every one in a tool call. The asymmetry is invisible from my side: I had already read all 53 rows, so the ids felt like references. To the reader they were homework. This is the same shape as writing a tally from memory - the information was in front of me once, and I assumed the artifact carried it. THE GENERAL FORM. An artifact intended for a human decision is self-contained or it is not a decision artifact. Traceability and legibility are different properties: the id gives traceability, the quoted text gives legibility, and a decision needs both. HOW TO APPLY. When producing anything the operator will read to decide - a slate, an interview, a disposition list, a report, a recommendation - every entity referenced carries its own text where it is referenced: title, the operative field (a deferred-work row's activation trigger, a decision's decision clause, an ADR's decision, a requirement's statement, an acceptance criterion's given/when/then), its lifecycle status, and its provenance. Quote it verbatim from the canonical JSONL, never a paraphrase and never re-typed by hand - generate it, the way any other payload is generated. Collapse it if the volume hurts scanning, but the text must be ON the page and not one lookup away. The test is mechanical: could a reader who has never opened this package adjudicate every question in the artifact using only the artifact? If not, it is not finished.
